Everyone knows the story. Protected lion killed by an American dentist in South Africa. He paid for it, and had the correct permits, but the curcumstamces surrounding it are shady. He also has had at least one big game hunt in the past where he lied and was fined. He's essentially gone into hiding. I personally don't think we'll get real answers unless he is extradited and tried alongside the guide and landowner, but wonder if the trial will be fair outside our constitutional borders. What do you folks think?

FYI - I think trophy hunting is cowardly and elitist. I despise it. This post is to gather people's opinion on the lawfulness of the act and whether or not he should be extradited to South Africa for trial.

A lot of the reaction about this story is fueled because people don't want to hear how someone killed a beautiful animal and the fact is that killing even an endangered species can be beneficial overall and even necessary under certain circumstances for maintaining a species. I am not saying that is what is involved in this story, but just wanted to throw that out there.

I also want to point out that everyone who's grabbed a torch and pitchfork wasn't there and doesn't know what happened. Having said that, I do agree this all smacks of shadiness, and I think everyone just needs to calm the fuck down and wait to see if we can hear what really happened. I realize that's like asking a bonobo to not rub one out, but hey, I can dream right?
That's why I'm trying to focus this on whether or not people feel he should be extradited or not. All other opinions aside, do people think this will lead to concrete answers or not.

If someone commits a crime here in the US and are from another country, they are punished based on our laws. Kill someone, go to jail and or die. He committed a crime in another country and therefore should be punished based on their laws. If killing a protected animal is grounds for execution, then so be it. If it's grounds for a billion dollar charge, so be it. Sentenced to execution for chewing gum in public would be inhumane, but we expect foreigners to abide by our laws, we need to abide by other country's laws while in said country.

I don't give an oink and I'm tired of seeing that shit plastered all over the place. Lions are not an endangered species, and the exorbitant hunting fees contribute to conservation efforts (though this is debatable in a country with rampant corruption like Zimbabwe). And the idea of extraditing this guy to Zimbabwe to face prison time in a country where its ruler basically eats a zoo for his birthday is beyond ludicrous.

http://www.eregulations.com/newhampshire/hunting2011/archive2010/youth-hunting-in-nh/ has some interesting information. At first I thought there was a minimum age requirement before someone could hunt but it appears any age under 16 and has to be with an adult hunter. So this sounds like a great deal. I was shooting a .22 at age 10 and kids at age 8 frequently shoot boar and deer in Texas from a stand. Obviously a young person likely would need assistance such as a bench rest. I said person for a reason: Much to my chagrin some women are much better shots than I am. Leave it to the BBC to sensationalize something to ridicule American hunters.

I got my Idaho lifetime hunting license as a high school graduation gift, and it was $300 or $400. Right now, an infant lifetime hunting license is less than $300. If my family would have had the money, it would have made more sense to buy me that lifetime license as an infant instead of paying $10 to $15 per year and THEN buying the $300 license. Idaho combination licenses are $1113 and $795, which saves you a little over $300 if you buy it before the kid turns 1.

And as pointed out in the article, the kid can't use the hunting portion of it until he meets all of the legal requirements for hunting in NH, which includes a minimum age and successful completion of a Hunter's Education course. Just like every other legal hunter in NH.
